questions.q: Why does the lesson run `pytest test_ask.py` separately from running `ask.py` itself with a real API key?
options: Because pytest cannot be run after the script itself has been executed
To confirm the tool's logic works correctly without needing a real credential or a live network call at all
Because the tests overwrite the API_KEY environment variable
Running tests and running the script must always happen in the same command
questions.explain: The whole point of mocking the network in the tests (Lesson 36) is that the test suite can verify the client's logic independent of any real credential or live connection — running it separately demonstrates that independence.

questions.q: Which lesson's pattern does setting `API_KEY` as an environment variable (rather than hard-coding it in the script) follow?
options: Lesson 25, Authentication Headers & API Keys
Lesson 13, Classes & Objects
Lesson 8, Lists & List Comprehensions
Lesson 29, asyncio Fundamentals
questions.explain: Lesson 25 (Chapter 5) covered authentication headers and API keys, including why credentials belong in environment variables rather than hard-coded in source code — the pattern this lesson's run-through follows.

questions.q: What does the lesson's suggested "async batch mode" next step involve?
options: Rewriting the whole tool in a different programming language
Removing all error handling to simplify the code
Switching from requests to a database connection
Using asyncio.gather(), from Lesson 30, to process a whole file of prompts concurrently instead of one at a time
questions.explain: The lesson suggests extending the tool to accept a file of multiple prompts and process them concurrently using the asyncio.gather() pattern from Lesson 30, rather than looping through them one at a time.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend emphasizing when describing this capstone project in an interview?
options: Reciting the exact line count of the final script
Only the total time it took to build
The decisions behind the code — why a class was used, why specific exceptions were caught, why tests mock the network — not just what the code does
Avoiding any mention of testing or error handling
questions.explain: The lesson specifically advises leading with the reasoning behind design choices (class vs. function, specific exception handling, mocked tests) rather than just narrating what the code does — interviewers remember candidates who can explain tradeoffs.
